'''Jerzy Władysław Jurka''' (June 4, 1950 – July 19, 2014) was a [[Polish American|Polish–American]] [[computational biology|computational]] and [[molecular biology|molecular]] biologist known for his pioneering work on [[repetitive DNA]] and [[transposable elements]] (TEs) in eukaryotic genomes.<ref name="GIRIInMemoriam">{{cite web |url=http://www.girinst.org/jurka_in_memoriam.html |title=In Memoriam: Dr. Jerzy Jurka (1950–2014) |publisher=Genetic Information Research Institute |accessdate=7 December 2024}}</ref><ref name="Obit"/> He served as the assistant director of research at the [[Linus Pauling Institute]] prior to founding and directing the [[Genetic Information Research Institute]] (GIRI) in [[Mountain View, California]].<ref name="OSUOral">{{cite web |url=http://scarc.library.oregonstate.edu/oh150/lpi/audio-lawson-20111215.html |title=An Oral History of the Linus Pauling Institute: Interview with Steven Lawson |publisher=Oregon State University |accessdate=7 December 2024}}</ref><ref name="GIRIInMemoriam"/>

== Early life and education ==
Jurka was born on June 4, 1950, in the village of [[Ponikiew, Lesser Poland Voivodeship|Ponikiew]], Poland.<ref name="GIRIInMemoriam"/> He obtained his M.Sc. in Chemistry from the [[Jagiellonian University]] and a D.Sc. in Molecular Biology from the [[University of Warsaw]].<ref name="GIRIInMemoriam"/> After earning his doctorate, Jurka moved to the United States and conducted post-doctoral research at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="GIRIInMemoriam"/>

== Career and research ==
After completing his post-doctoral research, Jurka joined the [[Linus Pauling Institute]] in Palo Alto, California, where he eventually served as assistant director of research.<ref name="OSUOral"/> During his tenure, he collaborated with several notable scientists, including [[Linus Pauling]], [[George Irving Bell]], [[Roy John Britten|Roy Britten]], [[Temple F. Smith|Temple Smith]], and [[Emile Zuckerkandl]].<ref name="OSUOral"/> In 1994, he founded the [[Genetic Information Research Institute]] (GIRI), focusing on the computational analysis of genome sequences and the identification of transposable elements.<ref name="GIRIInMemoriam"/>

Jurka’s team developed ''[[Repbase]]'', a widely used reference database of eukaryotic repetitive elements that aids in [[DNA annotation]] and comparative genomics.<ref name="Jurka2005">{{cite journal|vauthors=Jurka J, Kapitonov VV, Pavlicek A, Klonowski P, Kohany O, Jurka MV|title=Repbase Update, a database of eukaryotic repetitive elements|journal=Nucleic Acids Research|volume=33|issue=Database issue|pages=D142–D145|date=2005|doi=10.1093/nar/gki108|pmid=15608167|pmc=1087437}}</ref> His work on [[Alu element]]s, one of the most abundant short interspersed elements in primate genomes, provided insights into their classification, the mechanisms behind their proliferation, and their paternal transmission.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Jurka J, Smith T|title=A fundamental division in the Alu family of repeated sequences|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=85|issue=13|pages=4775–4778|date=July 1988|doi=10.1073/pnas.85.13.4775|doi-access=free |pmid=3387438|pmc=280518|bibcode=1988PNAS...85.4775J}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Jurka J|title=Sequence patterns indicate an enzymatic involvement in integration of mammalian retroposons|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=94|issue=5|pages=1872–1877|date=March 1997|doi=10.1073/pnas.94.5.1872|doi-access=free |pmid=9050872|pmc=20010|bibcode=1997PNAS...94.1872J}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Jurka J, etal|title=Active Alu elements are passed primarily through paternal germlines|journal=Theoretical Population Biology|volume=61|issue=4|pages=519–530|date=June 2002|doi=10.1006/tpbi.2002.1602|pmid=12167372}}</ref>

Jurka’s research group discovered and characterized numerous TE families. In collaboration with Vladimir Kapitonov, Jurka identified ''[[Helitron (biology)|Helitrons]]'', a family of rolling-circle transposons that influence genomic [[evolution]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Kapitonov VV|author2=Jurka J|title=Helitrons on a roll: eukaryotic rolling-circle transposons|journal=Trends in Genetics|volume=23|issue=10|pages=521–529|date=October 2007|doi=10.1016/j.tig.2007.08.004|pmid=17850916}}</ref> In 2006, they reported the discovery of [[Polinton]] (also known as Maverick) transposons, self-synthesizing DNA elements found in diverse eukaryotes, providing important clues about the structure and evolution of complex genomes.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Kapitonov VV|author2=Jurka J|title=Self-synthesizing DNA transposons in eukaryotes|journal=PNAS|volume=103|issue=12|pages=4540–4545|date=March 21, 2006|doi=10.1073/pnas.0600833103|doi-access=free |pmid=16537396|pmc=1450207|bibcode=2006PNAS..103.4540K}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Pritham EJ, Putivala T, Feschotte C|title=Mavericks, a novel class of giant transposable elements widespread in eukaryotes and related to DNA viruses|journal=Gene|volume=390|issue=1–2|pages=3–17|date=April 2007|doi=10.1016/j.gene.2006.08.008|pmid=17034960}}</ref>

Later, Jurka and colleagues linked TE family emergence to processes in classical [[population genetics]], proposing that population subdivision and [[speciation]] events could correlate with the distribution and diversification of transposable element families.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Jurka J, Bao W, Kojima K|title=Families of transposable elements, population structure and the origin of species|journal=Biology Direct|volume=6|issue=44|date=June 2011|page=44 |doi=10.1186/1745-6150-6-44|doi-access=free |pmid=21929767|pmc=3183009}}</ref>

Jurka’s [[Erdős number]] is 3, tracing a collaboration path through [[Temple F. Smith]] and [[Stanislaw Ulam]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://files.oakland.edu/users/grossman/enp/Erdos1.html|title=The Erdős Number Project|publisher=Oakland University|accessdate=7 December 2024}}</ref>
